---
title: "Health, Risk, and Public Evidence（健康、风险与公共证据）"
---

## Health, Wellbeing, and Daily Functioning（健康、福祉与日常功能）

Health（健康）is a state of complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing（身心健康）— a positive condition that allows people to function fully, pursue meaningful goals, and participate in community life. The World Health Organization's definition extends beyond the absence of disease（疾病的缺席）to encompass the full range of capacities that enable human flourishing（人的全面发展）. This broader conception shifts attention from treating illness to promoting the conditions — biological, psychological, social, and environmental — that allow people to thrive.

Wellbeing（福祉）refers to the overall quality of a person's life experience across multiple dimensions. It includes physical health（身体健康）, mental health（心理健康）, social connections（社会联系）, life satisfaction（生活满意度）, and the ability to pursue activities that provide meaning and purpose（意义和目标）. Wellbeing is influenced by many factors beyond medical care: income（收入）, education（教育）, housing（住房）, employment（就业）, social relationships（社会关系）, environmental quality（环境质量）, and personal safety（人身安全）. A person may be free from diagnosed disease but still experience low wellbeing if they are socially isolated（社会隔离的）, financially stressed（经济压力的）, living in unsafe conditions, or unable to participate in activities they value.

Daily functioning（日常功能）is the ability to perform the activities of everyday life independently and effectively. Basic activities of daily living（日常生活活动 / ADLs）include eating, bathing, dressing, toileting, and moving around — the fundamental self-care tasks（自我照顾任务）that determine whether a person can live independently. Instrumental activities of daily living（工具性日常生活活动 / IADLs）include more complex tasks — working, managing finances（管理财务）, preparing meals, using transportation, managing medications（管理药物）, and participating in social life. Health problems reduce daily functioning, and reduced functioning can in turn worsen health through a downward spiral（下降螺旋）: illness leads to inactivity（不活动）, inactivity leads to muscle weakness（肌肉无力）and cardiovascular decline（心血管功能下降）, which leads to further functional limitation（功能限制）and greater vulnerability to additional health problems.

The biopsychosocial model（生物心理社会模型）provides a framework for understanding health as the interaction of three domains of influence. Biological factors（生物因素）include genetics（遗传）, pathogens（病原体）, injuries（损伤）, physiological processes（生理过程）, and age-related changes（年龄相关变化）. Psychological factors（心理因素）include thoughts, emotions, behaviours, coping strategies（应对策略）, stress responses（压力反应）, and health beliefs（健康信念）. Social factors（社会因素）include income, education, social support（社会支持）, cultural context（文化背景）, access to healthcare（医疗保健的可及性）, and the physical environment. Health outcomes emerge from the interaction of all three domains — a person's genetic predisposition（遗传易感性）to heart disease may never lead to actual disease if their social environment and behaviours are protective, while a person with low genetic risk may develop illness due to chronic stress（慢性压力）, poor living conditions, and limited access to preventive care（预防性护理）.

The social determinants of health（健康的社会决定因素）are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age. These conditions are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels — by policy choices（政策选择）, economic systems（经济体系）, social norms（社会规范）, and historical patterns（历史模式）of inequality. The social gradient in health（健康的社会梯度）refers to the finding that health outcomes improve at every step up the socioeconomic ladder（社会经济阶梯）— each increment of income, education, and occupational status（职业地位）is associated with better health, from the poorest to the wealthiest. This gradient is not merely a comparison between the very poor and everyone else; it operates across the entire population, suggesting that the conditions of daily life — autonomy（自主性）, social participation（社会参与）, freedom from chronic stress, access to resources — shape health at every level of society.

Health therefore emerges from the interaction of biological, psychological, and social systems. The vocabulary of health — wellbeing, daily functioning, biopsychosocial model, social determinants of health, social gradient — describes how health is produced by the conditions in which people live, including the medical care they receive. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from social and environmental conditions through biological mechanisms to the health outcomes that determine how long and how well people live.

## Risk Factors and Probability（风险因素与概率）

A risk factor（风险因素）is any attribute, characteristic, or exposure that increases the probability（概率）of developing a disease or experiencing a negative health outcome. Risk factors operate at the population level（群体层面）— they increase probability across a group, but they do not determine individual outcomes with certainty. Some people with many risk factors remain healthy throughout their lives, while some people with no identifiable risk factors develop disease. This probabilistic nature（概率性质）of risk factors is essential to understanding how health research works, why individual cases cannot be predicted with certainty, and why public health interventions（公共健康干预）target populations rather than individuals.

Risk factors fall into several categories that interact and compound each other. Behavioural risk factors（行为风险因素）relate to personal choices and habits — smoking（吸烟）, diet（饮食）, physical activity（体力活动）, alcohol consumption（饮酒）, sleep patterns（睡眠模式）, and risk-taking behaviours（冒险行为）. These are modifiable（可改变的）— people can change them, though changing established behaviours is difficult because habits are embedded in daily routines, social contexts, and neural reward systems（神经奖励系统）. Biological risk factors（生物风险因素）relate to the body's characteristics — age, sex, genetics, blood pressure（血压）, cholesterol levels（胆固醇水平）, body weight（体重）, and inflammatory markers（炎症标志物）. Some biological risk factors are modifiable through behaviour or medication（药物）(blood pressure, cholesterol, weight), while others are fixed（固定的）(age, sex, genetic inheritance). Environmental risk factors（环境风险因素）relate to the physical and social environment — air pollution（空气污染）, water quality（水质）, workplace hazards（工作场所危害）, neighbourhood safety（社区安全）, and social support. These are often beyond individual control and require policy interventions（政策干预）and structural changes（结构性变革）to address.

Probability is expressed in health research using several measures that convey different information. Absolute risk（绝对风险）is the probability of an event occurring in a defined population over a specified time period. If 5 out of 100 smokers develop lung cancer（肺癌）over 10 years, the absolute risk is 5 percent. Relative risk（相对风险）compares the probability in an exposed group（暴露组）to the probability in an unexposed group（非暴露组）. If 5 percent of smokers and 0.3 percent of non-smokers develop lung cancer, the relative risk is 5 / 0.3 ≈ 16.7 — smokers have approximately seventeen times the risk of non-smokers. Relative risk can appear dramatic even when absolute risk is small: a relative risk of 2.0 for a disease with an absolute risk of 0.01 percent means the risk increases to 0.02 percent — a doubling that sounds alarming but represents a very small absolute change（绝对变化）. Understanding both measures is essential for evaluating health claims accurately.

Odds ratio（比值比）is another measure used in health research, particularly in case-control studies（病例对照研究）where absolute risk cannot be calculated directly because the researcher selects the number of cases and controls rather than observing natural frequencies. The odds ratio compares the odds of exposure（暴露的几率）among cases (people with the disease) to the odds of exposure among controls (people without the disease). An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that exposure is more common among cases than controls, suggesting a potential risk factor. When the disease is rare, the odds ratio approximates the relative risk; when the disease is common, the odds ratio overestimates the relative risk.

Attributable risk（归因风险）measures how much of the disease burden（疾病负担）in a population can be attributed to a specific risk factor. If smoking is responsible for 85 percent of lung cancer cases in a population, the population attributable fraction（人群归因分数）is 85 percent. This measure is particularly useful for public health planning（公共健康规划）because it tells policymakers how much disease could potentially be prevented if the risk factor were eliminated, allowing them to prioritise interventions based on their potential population-level impact（群体层面影响）.

Risk communication（风险沟通）is challenging because people systematically misunderstand probability and risk. They overestimate small risks that are dramatic, memorable, or emotionally vivid（情感生动的）— rare diseases, plane crashes, terrorist attacks — and underestimate large risks that are common, gradual, and less dramatic — heart disease, stroke, diabetes. They struggle to distinguish absolute from relative risk, making them vulnerable to misleading health claims（误导性健康声明）. A pharmaceutical advertisement（药品广告）stating that a drug "reduces heart attack risk by 50 percent" sounds impressive, but if the absolute risk reduction（绝对风险降低）is from 2 percent to 1 percent, the benefit is much smaller than the relative figure suggests. Effective risk communication presents both absolute and relative measures, uses natural frequencies（自然频率）rather than percentages where possible, and provides context that helps people compare risks meaningfully.

Risk factors therefore represent the mechanism through which health researchers identify the causes of disease and quantify their effects at the population level. The vocabulary of risk — risk factor, absolute risk, relative risk, odds ratio, attributable risk, modifiable risk factor, probability — names the measures through which health researchers quantify the relationship between exposures and health outcomes and the communication challenges that arise when translating these measures for public understanding. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from risk factor identification through probability estimation to the public health decisions that determine which risk factors are targeted for intervention and how those interventions are communicated to the public.

## Diet, Exercise, Sleep, and Stress（饮食、运动、睡眠与压力）

Diet（饮食）provides the nutrients（营养素）the body needs to maintain cellular function（细胞功能）, build and repair tissues（构建和修复组织）, produce energy（产生能量）, and support immune function（免疫功能）. Macronutrients（宏量营养素）— carbohydrates（碳水化合物）, proteins（蛋白质）, and fats（脂肪）— provide energy and structural materials. Micronutrients（微量营养素）— vitamins（维生素）and minerals（矿物质）— serve as cofactors（辅因子）for metabolic processes（代谢过程）: vitamin C is needed for collagen synthesis（胶原蛋白合成）, iron（铁）for oxygen transport（氧气运输）, calcium（钙）for bone structure（骨骼结构）and nerve signalling（神经信号传导）, and zinc（锌）for immune cell function（免疫细胞功能）. Fibre（膳食纤维）supports digestive health（消化健康）, regulates blood sugar（血糖）and cholesterol（胆固醇）, and feeds beneficial gut bacteria（有益肠道细菌）.

Dietary patterns（膳食模式）affect health through multiple interacting mechanisms. A diet high in ultra-processed foods（超加工食品）, added sugar（添加糖）, refined carbohydrates（精制碳水化合物）, and unhealthy fats（不健康脂肪）increases the risk of obesity（肥胖）, type 2 diabetes（2型糖尿病）, cardiovascular disease（心血管疾病）, and certain cancers（特定癌症）. These effects are mediated through chronic inflammation（慢性炎症）, oxidative stress（氧化应激）, insulin resistance（胰岛素抵抗）, dyslipidaemia（血脂异常）, and disruption of the gut microbiome（肠道微生物组紊乱）. A diet rich in vegetables（蔬菜）, fruits（水果）, whole grains（全谷物）, legumes（豆类）, lean protein（瘦肉蛋白）, and healthy fats provides protective nutrients（保护性营养素）, bioactive compounds（生物活性化合物）, and fibre that reduce inflammation, improve metabolic function（代谢功能）, and support a diverse and resilient gut microbiome.

Exercise（运动）improves health through multiple physiological mechanisms（生理机制）that operate across different body systems（身体系统）. Regular physical activity strengthens the heart muscle（心肌）, improves blood vessel elasticity（血管弹性）, lowers resting blood pressure（静息血压）, and improves lipid profiles（血脂谱）. It improves glucose metabolism（葡萄糖代谢）by increasing insulin sensitivity（胰岛素敏感性）in muscle and liver cells. It helps maintain healthy body weight by increasing energy expenditure（能量消耗）and preserving lean muscle mass（瘦体重）during weight loss. It strengthens bones（骨骼）through mechanical loading（机械负荷）, reducing the risk of osteoporosis（骨质疏松）and fractures（骨折）in older adults. Exercise also improves mental health（心理健康）by reducing symptoms of anxiety（焦虑）and depression（抑郁）, improving mood（情绪）, enhancing cognitive function（认知功能）through increased cerebral blood flow（脑血流）and stimulation of neurotrophic factors（神经营养因子）that support neuron growth（神经元生长）and survival.

The dose-response relationship（剂量-反应关系）between exercise and health is curvilinear（曲线性的）. The greatest health benefits come from moving from a sedentary state（久坐状态）to moderate activity（中等强度活动）— the first 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week produce the largest risk reductions（风险降低）for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and all-cause mortality（全因死亡率）. Additional activity provides additional benefits, but the marginal gains（边际收益）diminish at higher volumes. This curvilinear relationship means that even small increases in physical activity produce meaningful health improvements for sedentary individuals — a finding with important public health implications（公共健康意义）because it suggests that the most beneficial intervention targets the least active population members.

Sleep（睡眠）is a complex physiological process（复杂生理过程）essential for health that occupies approximately one-third of human life. During sleep, the body repairs tissues（修复组织）, consolidates memories（巩固记忆）through replay and synaptic strengthening（突触强化）, regulates hormones（调节激素）including growth hormone（生长激素）and cortisol（皮质醇）, and clears metabolic waste products（代谢废物）from the brain through the glymphatic system（类淋巴系统）— a recently discovered waste clearance pathway that is most active during deep sleep（深度睡眠）. Chronic sleep deprivation（慢性睡眠剥夺）disrupts all of these processes, increasing the risk of obesity (through effects on appetite-regulating hormones / 食欲调节激素), diabetes (through impaired glucose metabolism), cardiovascular disease (through elevated blood pressure and inflammation), depression, impaired immune function（免疫功能受损）, and cognitive decline（认知衰退）.

Stress（压力）is the body's coordinated response to demands or threats — the fight-or-flight response（战斗或逃跑反应）that prepares the organism for immediate action. This response involves activation of the sympathetic nervous system（交感神经系统）and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis（下丘脑-垂体-肾上腺轴）, releasing stress hormones（压力激素）including cortisol and adrenaline（肾上腺素）. Short-term stress can be adaptive — it motivates action, improves performance in challenging situations, sharpens attention, and helps the body respond to immediate threats. Chronic stress（慢性压力）— stress that persists for weeks, months, or years — becomes maladaptive（适应不良的）. Sustained activation of the stress response elevates blood pressure, suppresses immune function（抑制免疫功能）, increases abdominal fat storage（腹部脂肪储存）, disrupts sleep, contributes to anxiety and depression, and accelerates biological aging（生物衰老）.

The allostatic load（适应负荷）model describes how chronic stress accumulates physiological damage over time. Each stress response causes wear and tear（磨损）on the body's regulatory systems. When stress responses are activated too frequently or for too long — due to poverty, discrimination（歧视）, caregiving burden（照护负担）, job strain（工作紧张）, or social isolation — this wear and tear accumulates, leading to physiological dysregulation（生理失调）that increases disease risk across multiple organ systems（器官系统）. Allostatic load can be measured through biomarkers（生物标志物）including blood pressure, cortisol patterns, inflammatory markers（炎症标志物）, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels. People with high allostatic load scores have higher rates of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cognitive decline, and mortality — demonstrating that the cumulative biological cost of chronic stress translates into measurable health outcomes.

Diet, exercise, sleep, and stress are interconnected through multiple feedback loops（反馈循环）that create cascading effects in both directions. Poor sleep increases cortisol, which promotes unhealthy food cravings（不健康的食物渴望）for high-sugar and high-fat foods and reduces motivation for exercise. Lack of exercise reduces sleep quality（睡眠质量）and increases stress reactivity（压力反应性）. Chronic stress disrupts eating patterns（饮食模式）and sleep architecture（睡眠结构）. Improving any one factor can initiate a positive cascade（正向级联）: better sleep reduces stress, which improves dietary choices, which increases energy for exercise, which further improves sleep quality. This interconnectedness means that lifestyle interventions（生活方式干预）that address multiple factors simultaneously may be more effective than interventions targeting single behaviours in isolation.

Diet, exercise, sleep, and stress therefore represent the daily behaviours and physiological processes that interact to shape health outcomes. The vocabulary of lifestyle health — diet, exercise, sleep architecture, REM sleep, fight-or-flight response, chronic stress, allostatic load, dose-response relationship — names the mechanisms through which daily behaviours and physiological processes interact to shape health outcomes. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from daily behaviours through physiological mechanisms to the health outcomes that determine whether people develop chronic disease or maintain good health across their lifespan.

## Prevention and Public Health（预防与公共健康）

Prevention（预防）refers to actions taken to avoid disease or injury before it occurs or before it progresses to a more serious stage. Prevention is generally more effective and less costly than treatment（治疗）— it avoids the suffering, disability, and expense of disease rather than attempting to reverse damage after it has developed. Prevention operates at three levels that target different stages of the disease process（疾病过程）.

Primary prevention（一级预防）prevents disease from developing by addressing risk factors before any pathology（病理变化）exists. Vaccination（疫苗接种）prevents infectious diseases（传染病）by training the immune system（免疫系统）to recognise and respond to pathogens before exposure occurs. Healthy diet and regular exercise prevent chronic diseases（慢性病）by maintaining healthy body weight, blood pressure, blood sugar, and lipid levels. Tobacco control（烟草控制）— including taxation（税收）, advertising bans（广告禁令）, smoke-free policies（无烟政策）, and cessation programmes（戒烟项目）— prevents lung cancer, heart disease, and respiratory diseases by reducing smoking initiation（吸烟起始）and promoting quitting. Primary prevention addresses the root causes（根本原因）of disease and produces the largest population health gains per dollar spent.

Secondary prevention（二级预防）detects disease at an early stage when treatment is more effective and less invasive（侵入性的）. Screening tests（筛查检测）— mammograms（乳腺X线检查）for breast cancer（乳腺癌）, colonoscopy（结肠镜检查）for colorectal cancer（结直肠癌）, blood pressure checks（血压检测）for hypertension（高血压）, blood glucose tests（血糖检测）for diabetes, and cervical smears（宫颈涂片）for cervical cancer（宫颈癌）— identify disease before symptoms appear. Early detection allows treatment at a stage when the disease is more responsive to intervention, improving survival rates（存活率）, reducing the need for aggressive treatments（激进治疗）, and preserving quality of life. The effectiveness of screening depends on the test's sensitivity（灵敏度）— its ability to correctly identify people who have the disease — and specificity（特异度）— its ability to correctly identify people who do not have the disease.

Tertiary prevention（三级预防）manages established disease to prevent complications（并发症）, reduce disability（残疾）, and improve quality of life. Cardiac rehabilitation programmes（心脏康复项目）help people recover after heart attacks（心脏病发作）and reduce the risk of recurrent events（复发事件）. Medication adherence（药物依从性）prevents complications of diabetes, hypertension, and HIV. Physical therapy（物理治疗）prevents disability after stroke（中风）or injury. Palliative care（姑息治疗）manages symptoms and maintains quality of life for people with advanced disease. Tertiary prevention does not prevent the disease itself but reduces its impact on the person's life and prevents secondary health problems.

Public health（公共健康）is the science and practice of protecting and improving the health of populations through organised societal effort. Unlike clinical medicine（临床医学）, which treats individuals one at a time, public health focuses on the conditions that affect entire populations — the social, environmental, economic, and behavioural factors that determine health at scale. Public health interventions include vaccination programmes, clean water supply（清洁供水）, food safety regulations（食品安全法规）, sanitation systems（卫生系统）, tobacco and alcohol control, road safety regulations（道路安全法规）, health education campaigns（健康教育运动）, and disease surveillance（疾病监测）. These population-level interventions often produce larger health gains than clinical medicine because they reach entire populations simultaneously rather than treating individuals who seek care — the introduction of clean water and sanitation in the nineteenth century prevented more deaths than any medical treatment developed in the same period.

Vaccination is one of the most effective public health interventions in human history. Vaccines work by exposing the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen — an inactivated virus（灭活病毒）, a protein fragment（蛋白片段）, or a weakened live organism（减毒活体）— training it to recognise and mount a rapid defence（快速防御）if the actual pathogen is encountered later. Vaccination has eradicated smallpox（天花）, nearly eliminated polio（脊髓灰质炎）, and dramatically reduced the burden of measles（麻疹）, tetanus（破伤风）, diphtheria（白喉）, hepatitis B（乙型肝炎）, and many other infectious diseases. Herd immunity（群体免疫）occurs when a sufficiently high proportion of the population is vaccinated — typically 85 to 95 percent depending on the disease — that even unvaccinated individuals are protected because the pathogen cannot spread effectively through the population. Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated — newborns（新生儿）, immunocompromised individuals（免疫功能低下者）, and people with medical contraindications（医学禁忌症）— making vaccination a collective responsibility（集体责任）as well as an individual health decision.

Prevention and public health therefore represent the mechanisms through which disease can be prevented at the individual and population levels through interventions that address causes rather than waiting for disease to develop. The vocabulary of prevention and public health — primary prevention, secondary prevention, tertiary prevention, screening, vaccination, herd immunity, non-communicable disease, population health — names the strategies through which societies attempt to prevent disease before it occurs and the collective actions that protect entire populations from health threats. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from prevention strategies through population-level interventions to the health outcomes that determine whether societies can reduce the burden of disease and increase the healthy lifespan of their populations.

## Medical Evidence and Study Findings（医学证据与研究发现）

Medical evidence（医学证据）supports or refutes claims about health, disease, and treatment. It comes from research studies that test treatments, interventions, diagnostic tests（诊断检测）, and risk factors using systematic methods. The quality of medical evidence varies substantially across study designs（研究设计）, and understanding the hierarchy of evidence（证据层级）is essential for evaluating health claims critically.

The randomised controlled trial（随机对照试验 / RCT）provides the strongest evidence for whether a treatment causes improvement. In an RCT, participants are randomly assigned（随机分配）to receive either the treatment being tested or a placebo（安慰剂）or standard treatment（标准治疗）. Random assignment ensures that the groups are similar in all important characteristics — age, sex, health status, disease severity（疾病严重程度）, socioeconomic factors — so that any difference in outcomes between groups can be attributed to the treatment rather than to pre-existing differences. The placebo control accounts for the placebo effect（安慰剂效应）— improvements that occur because patients believe they are receiving treatment, activate expectations of recovery（康复期望）, and experience physiological changes driven by those expectations rather than by any pharmacological action（药理作用）.

Blinding（盲法）reduces bias（偏见）in RCTs at multiple levels. In a single-blind trial（单盲试验）, participants do not know whether they are receiving the treatment or placebo, preventing their expectations from influencing reported outcomes. In a double-blind trial（双盲试验）, neither participants nor the researchers who interact with them and assess outcomes know the treatment assignment. Blinding prevents researcher expectations（研究者期望）from influencing how they interpret ambiguous symptoms, how they encourage participants, or how they measure outcomes. In some studies, a third level of blinding extends to the data analysts（数据分析人员）, who do not know which group is which until after the analysis is complete. The absence of blinding can inflate（夸大）treatment effects by 10 to 30 percent, making blinded trials essential for unbiased evidence.

Observational studies（观察性研究）observe groups of people over time and measure health outcomes without assigning treatments. Cohort studies（队列研究）follow a group of people forward in time（前瞻性）, comparing outcomes between those exposed and not exposed to a risk factor or behaviour. The Framingham Heart Study（弗雷明汉心脏研究）followed thousands of residents for decades, establishing that smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and obesity increase cardiovascular disease risk. Case-control studies（病例对照研究）compare people with a disease (cases) to people without it (controls), looking backward（回顾性）to identify differences in past exposures. Observational studies can identify associations（关联）between risk factors and health outcomes across large populations over long periods — questions that RCTs cannot address because it would be unethical to randomly assign people to smoke or because the outcomes take decades to develop. Observational studies cannot prove causation（因果关系）because confounding factors（混杂因素）— variables associated with both the exposure and the outcome — may explain the observed association.

Confounding（混杂）occurs when a third factor is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, creating a spurious（虚假的）or distorted association. Observational studies found that women taking hormone replacement therapy（激素替代疗法 / HRT）had lower rates of heart disease, leading to widespread recommendation of HRT for cardiovascular protection. Later RCTs found the opposite — HRT actually increased heart disease risk. The observational studies were confounded by socioeconomic status（社会经济地位）: women who chose to take HRT were wealthier, more educated, and had healthier lifestyles than those who did not, and it was their socioeconomic advantage — not the HRT — that protected their hearts. This example illustrates why observational evidence, however consistent, requires confirmation through experimental evidence（实验证据）before causal claims can be made confidently.

A systematic review（系统综述）combines the results of multiple studies on the same question using explicit, reproducible methods（明确的、可重复的方法）to identify, evaluate, and synthesise all relevant evidence. By pooling data（汇总数据）from many studies, systematic reviews provide more reliable evidence than any single study because they aggregate across different samples, settings, and methodologies. Meta-analysis（荟萃分析）is a statistical technique used in systematic reviews to combine quantitative results from different studies into a single summary estimate（汇总估计）. Meta-analysis increases statistical power（统计功效）, can detect effects that individual studies were too small to identify, and reveals heterogeneity（异质性）— differences in results across studies that may indicate important moderating factors（调节因素）such as population characteristics, treatment dosage（治疗剂量）, or study quality.

Medical evidence therefore represents the mechanism through which researchers determine whether treatments work and what causes disease. The vocabulary of medical evidence — randomised controlled trial, placebo, blinding, double-blind, observational study, cohort study, case-control study, confounding, systematic review, meta-analysis — names the study designs that produce evidence about health and treatment and the methodological standards that determine whether that evidence is trustworthy. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from study design through evidence evaluation to the conclusions that determine whether medical claims about treatments and risk factors are supported by rigorous empirical evidence.

## Association, Causation, and Caution（相关、因果与谨慎表达）

In health research, association（相关性）and causation（因果关系）are distinct concepts that are frequently conflated（混淆）in public discussion and media reporting. An association means that two variables are statistically related — when one changes, the other tends to change in a predictable direction. An association alone is insufficient to establish that one variable causes the other, because multiple alternative explanations（替代解释）can produce the same statistical pattern.

A study might find an association between coffee consumption（咖啡消费）and lower risk of heart disease（心脏病）. Several explanations are possible. Coffee might contain compounds that protect against heart disease (causation / 因果关系). People who drink coffee might have other characteristics that protect their hearts — they might be more physically active, have higher incomes, or have other healthy habits that explain the association (confounding / 混杂). The association might reflect reverse causation（反向因果）— people with heart disease might reduce their coffee consumption after diagnosis, making it appear that non-drinkers have more heart disease. Or the association might be coincidental（巧合的）, particularly if it emerged from a study that tested many associations simultaneously.

The Bradford Hill criteria（布拉德福德·希尔标准）provide a framework for evaluating whether an observed association is likely to be causal. These criteria include: strength of association（关联强度）— larger effects are less likely to be explained entirely by confounding; consistency（一致性）— the association is found across different studies, populations, methods, and time periods; specificity（特异性）— the exposure is associated with a specific outcome rather than with many unrelated outcomes; temporality（时间顺序）— the cause precedes the effect in time, which is the only absolutely necessary criterion; biological gradient（生物梯度）— more exposure leads to more effect in a dose-response relationship（剂量-反应关系）; plausibility（合理性）— a plausible biological mechanism（合理的生物学机制）exists; coherence（连贯性）— the finding is consistent with existing knowledge from other sources; experiment（实验证据）— experimental evidence supports the causal claim; and analogy（类比）— similar exposures produce similar effects in related contexts.

No single criterion is necessary or sufficient for establishing causation. The causal link between smoking and lung cancer（吸烟与肺癌的因果关系）was accepted before all criteria were fully satisfied because the association was strong (smokers had approximately twenty times the risk), consistent (found across dozens of studies in different countries), specific (smoking was most strongly associated with lung cancer rather than with all diseases equally), temporal (smoking preceded cancer development), and showed a clear dose-response relationship (more cigarettes per day and more years of smoking produced higher risk). The biological mechanism（生物学机制）— carcinogenic compounds（致癌化合物）in tobacco smoke damaging lung cell DNA（肺细胞DNA）— was identified later but confirmed the epidemiological evidence（流行病学证据）.

Health writing uses cautious language（谨慎表达）because establishing causation is difficult, single studies rarely provide definitive evidence, and premature causal claims can mislead clinical practice and public policy. Common expressions include: "The evidence suggests that..." — indicating that the evidence points in a direction but remains open to alternative interpretations（替代解释）. "This finding is consistent with..." — indicating that the result does not contradict the hypothesis but does not confirm it definitively. "Further research is needed to confirm..." — explicitly acknowledging that the current evidence is insufficient for a firm conclusion. "There is an association between X and Y..." — carefully distinguishing correlation from causation. "X may increase the risk of Y..." — using modal verbs（情态动词）to express uncertainty（不确定性）rather than stating the relationship as established fact.

This caution reflects the scientific understanding that health is complex, that multiple factors interact to produce outcomes, and that single studies — however well-designed — represent one piece of a larger evidence base（证据基础）. The reader who understands these conventions can assess the strength of evidence behind health claims, distinguish between preliminary findings（初步发现）and well-established conclusions（已确立的结论）, and evaluate whether media reports（媒体报道）accurately represent the original research or overstate its implications.

Association and causation therefore represent the distinction between correlations that are coincidental and those that reflect genuine causal relationships. The vocabulary of causation — association, causation, Bradford Hill criteria, dose-response relationship, temporality, confounding, reverse causation, cautious language — names the framework through which health researchers distinguish between correlations that are coincidental and those that reflect genuine causal relationships. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from observed associations through causal evaluation to the conclusions that determine whether health claims about risk factors and treatments are supported by evidence that establishes causation or merely correlation.

## Population Health and Policy Response（群体健康与政策回应）

Population health（群体健康）refers to the health outcomes of a defined group of people — a community, a region, a nation, or a demographic category（人口类别）— rather than the health of individual patients. It is measured by indicators（指标）such as life expectancy（预期寿命）, infant mortality（婴儿死亡率）, maternal mortality（孕产妇死亡率）, disease prevalence（患病率）, disability-adjusted life years（伤残调整生命年 / DALYs）, and self-reported health status（自报健康状况）. These indicators vary greatly between countries and between different groups within the same country, reflecting differences in social, economic, environmental, and healthcare conditions.

Life expectancy at birth（出生时预期寿命）is one of the most widely used population health indicators. It estimates how many years a newborn can expect to live if current age-specific mortality rates（年龄别死亡率）remain constant throughout their life. Life expectancy has increased dramatically over the last century in most countries, driven primarily by reductions in infant and child mortality（婴儿和儿童死亡率）through vaccination, clean water, improved nutrition, and basic healthcare. Advances in treating cardiovascular disease（心血管疾病治疗）and cancer（癌症治疗）have extended life expectancy further in wealthy countries. However, life expectancy varies by more than thirty years between the healthiest and least healthy countries, and within countries it varies systematically by income, education, race, and geographic region — reflecting the social gradient in health（健康的社会梯度）.

Infant mortality（婴儿死亡率）— the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births — is a particularly sensitive indicator of population health because it reflects maternal health（母体健康）, access to prenatal care（产前护理）, nutrition（营养）, sanitation（卫生设施）, clean water, and the quality of healthcare delivery（医疗服务质量）. Countries with high infant mortality rates typically have broader health system weaknesses（卫生系统薄弱）that affect the entire population. Reducing infant mortality has been a major focus of global health efforts（全球健康努力）, and substantial progress has been achieved through vaccination, oral rehydration therapy（口服补液疗法）, improved maternal nutrition, and skilled birth attendance（熟练接生）.

Health inequality（健康不平等）refers to systematic, avoidable differences in health outcomes between population groups. In almost every country, people with lower income, less education, and lower social status have worse health outcomes — higher mortality, more chronic disease, greater disability, and shorter life expectancy — than people with higher socioeconomic status. These inequalities are not natural or inevitable — they result from social and economic policies that distribute resources, opportunities, and power unequally. The magnitude of health inequality varies across countries with similar levels of economic development, suggesting that policy choices（政策选择）— healthcare systems, social safety nets（社会安全网）, education access, labour market regulations（劳动市场监管）— significantly affect how health is distributed.

Health policy（健康政策）refers to decisions, plans, and actions undertaken by governments and institutions to achieve specific health goals at the population level. Health policy addresses healthcare funding（医疗资金）and delivery（医疗服务提供）, disease prevention, health promotion（健康促进）, regulation of food（食品监管）and pharmaceuticals（药品监管）, environmental protection（环境保护）, occupational health（职业健康）, and health research funding. Policy decisions shape the conditions that determine population health — the quality of air and water, the safety of food and workplaces, the accessibility of healthcare, the affordability of healthy choices, and the distribution of social and economic resources.

Governments use different policy tools to improve population health, each targeting different determinants and operating through different mechanisms. Taxation（税收）discourages unhealthy behaviours — tobacco taxes（烟草税）reduce smoking rates, sugar-sweetened beverage taxes（含糖饮料税）reduce consumption of added sugars, and carbon taxes（碳税）reduce pollution that damages respiratory health. Regulation（监管）requires healthy practices — mandatory seatbelt laws（强制安全带法）reduce traffic fatalities（交通死亡）, food labelling requirements（食品标签要求）help consumers make informed choices, and building codes（建筑规范）prevent exposure to lead（铅）and asbestos（石棉）. Investment in public services（公共服务投资）— clean water, sanitation, healthcare infrastructure, education, public transport — improves health at the population level by addressing the social and environmental conditions that determine health outcomes. Each policy tool addresses different determinants of health, operates through different causal pathways（因果路径）, and has different evidence supporting its effectiveness.

Population health and policy response therefore represent the mechanisms through which health is distributed across populations and how policy can improve health at the societal level. The vocabulary of population health — life expectancy, infant mortality, health inequality, health policy, social determinants, population-level intervention — names the indicators through which health is measured at the population level and the policy tools that shape the conditions determining health outcomes. Health texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from social and economic conditions through policy interventions to the population health outcomes that determine whether societies can reduce health inequalities and improve the health of all their members.
